doc.title: Shelly Berg interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Early piano, jam sessions at home and first gigs
summary: Music was always his path; he played Alley Cat at five, his father (trumpeter, French horn) hosted jam sessions, and Shelly began gigging at ten and sat in at jam sessions by fifteen.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: No I mean literally my earliest recollection is that music was going to be my thing. I don’t recall a time in my life ever that music wasn’t going to be my thing. I started picking out tunes at the piano when I was a toddler. And my parents came in when I was about five one day and I was playing “Alley Cat” with two hands. And so they decided it was time for lessons. So it’s always been me. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
This begs a trivia question. You might be one of the few people who knows who the guy who recorded “Alley Cat” is.
Oh no. I wasn’t able to read the liner notes at that age.
All right. I’ll tell you later. It’s an interesting name. So they recognized your talent?
Did they help you out in that regard?

Yeah, my dad is an avocational jazz trumpet player. And he was also a classical French horn player. So the music was always around me. There were always jam sessions at my house when I was a kid and if people were in off the road they usually ended up at our house a jam session and dinner. So yeah, they were very encouraging.
At that time it was Cleveland, Ohio. And I think by the time I was ten or eleven my dad had pretty well scoped out that I was a potential live-in accompanist for his jazz trumpet.
So he was bringing me along quickly. That was good.
Yeah. Do you recall the first time you played out?

Oh yeah. I started to play out doing shows and things when I was ten or eleven doing little paid gigs just kind of playing things that I’d worked out. And then by the time I was thirteen I was trying to go to jam sessions with my dad, and getting kicked off the stand. You know they’d let me play a half of a tune or a tune and then say now go, you’re done. But by the time I was fifteen I was in at the jam sessions I was playing.
